about: Wave-10 day-0 fixture (tpm-plan-wave10 rev 2 §1(b)). Data only; nothing here is a grade.

bell.line: Under Four Minutes: The Bell account comes across Milo's queue. He zeroes Halvard Bell's tenure, initials the form and sends him under by lunch, and Facilities clears the desk before the coffee finishes. When he asks where Bell goes, Zara tells him to write 'under' and nothing else, and Milo locks the ledger in his drawer without knowing why.

nodes.title: Retained
nodes.summary: Milo wakes in the intake atrium, where Prava tells him he is a strong culture fit, and starts in Reconciliations across the partition from Zara. She trains him with flat courtesy and tells him to read the appendices and thank no one. He learns the quota, the gray coffee and the newsletter, and is delighted to be useful.

children.title: Laminated
children.summary: Milo opens his eyes in the intake atrium, and Prava slides a laminated org chart across the desk and tells him he has been retained as a strong culture fit. He says yes before anyone offers a choice, and feels useful for the first time in decades.
children.setting: The intake atrium of the Undeath Pipeline

children.title: Across the Partition
children.summary: In Reconciliations, Milo pitches his hit-the-ground-running energy to Zara. She gives him one flat instruction, to close what is in his queue and open nothing else, and tells him to read the appendices and thank no one. He mistakes her courtesy for the start of a friendship.
children.setting: Reconciliations, a long room the colour of old teeth

children.title: Culture
children.summary: At the coffee station Milo learns the rest: the quota, the gray liquid the dead drink out of habit, the newsletter everyone agrees is the worst part, and all-hands graduation with confetti that dissolves before it lands. Old Fen remarks without looking up that nobody reads the appendices, and that this is what they are for. Milo resolves to be very good here.
children.setting: The coffee station and the all-hands amphitheater in the Marrow District

nodes.title: The Bell Account
nodes.summary: Milo closes Halvard Bell's restructured account in under four minutes, is summoned by Edric Thane, and stands rather than sit while the Lich tells him he was retained for not asking questions. Back at his desk he finds that Bell's tenure was moved rather than zeroed, and Zara tells him he has finally read an appendix.

children.title: Under Four Minutes
children.summary: The Bell account comes across Milo's queue. He zeroes Halvard Bell's tenure, initials the form and sends him under by lunch, and Facilities clears the desk before the coffee finishes. When he asks where Bell goes, Zara tells him to write 'under' and nothing else, and Milo locks the ledger in his drawer without knowing why.
children.setting: Milo's desk in Reconciliations

children.title: Heavy Paper
children.summary: A memo signed by Edric Thane summons Milo, who reads it as a career signal. Zara tells him to bring nothing, sign nothing, and stand if he is offered a chair. For the first time her flat calm sounds like a warning, not a habit.
children.setting: Reconciliations

children.title: The Corner Office
children.summary: In the cold corner office Milo stays standing and surprises himself. Edric calls his four-minute closure appetite rather than diligence, and tells him he was retained for not asking questions but should not mistake that for the reason he will be kept. Milo leaves knowing the Lich is watching him in particular.
children.setting: The corner office at the top of Aeon Holdings

children.title: The Unexplained Column
children.summary: Milo unlocks the ledger and finds that in a column no one ever explained, Bell's tenure was not zeroed but moved. He brings the discrepancy to Zara. She looks at it for a long time and tells him that now he has read an appendix and they have a great deal of paperwork to do: the discrepancy is real, and something at the top is drinking from it.
children.setting: Milo's desk in Reconciliations

nodes.title: Where the Numbers Go
nodes.summary: Following the column no one explained, Milo traces tenure from every sent-under account to a single pooled account at the top of the org chart and understands that the souls are harvested to keep the Lich continuing. His first instinct is to write it up as a process improvement and send it upstairs.

children.title: Follow the Column
children.summary: After hours, Milo pulls every sent-under account he has closed and follows the unexplained column. Halvard Bell's tenure, and everyone else's, flows the same way, and what he took for a single error becomes a pattern.
children.setting: Milo's desk in Reconciliations, after hours
children.tone: Absorbed, the old thrill of a good spreadsheet curdling

children.title: The Top of the Org Chart
children.summary: The flows converge on a single pooled account at the top of the org chart. Zara confirms it without explaining: the souls are not destroyed, they are harvested, and their tenure keeps Edric Thane continuing. Milo understands that the monstrous side effect is the business.
children.setting: Reconciliations, across the partition

children.title: Process Improvement
children.summary: Milo's forty-one years of instinct take over. He drafts a tidy report on the discrepancy, complete with recommendations, written to be useful and seen upstairs. Zara reads the subject line and says nothing, and her silence does not feel like approval.
children.setting: Milo's desk

threads: Milo's urge to optimize and climb

nodes.title: People in the Margins
nodes.summary: While Zara lets him sit with his draft report, Milo learns what his work costs. Prava keeps a forbidden ledger of eleven thousand names and weeps at graduation, Old Fen is content to file himself, and the Retention team's cheer hides despair. Edric's summons comes again, and the climb is now on offer. Milo cannot stand himself, tears up the report, and asks Zara what the alternative is; she shows him the signature sheet for a union of the dead.

children.title: Eleven Thousand Names
children.summary: Milo seeks out Prava at intake and finds the private ledger she is not allowed to keep, with the name of every one of the eleven thousand souls she has onboarded. At the quarter's all-hands graduation he watches her weep silently as the confetti dissolves, and for the first time his work has names.
children.setting: The intake atrium, then the all-hands amphitheater

children.title: Content
children.summary: In Records, Old Fen files without looking up and is perfectly at peace. Milo envies him, then realises that contentment is the end state the Pipeline wants for him too. Passing Retention, he hears its cheerful team talk the wavering back onto schedule and sees how despairing they are.
children.setting: Records and the Retention floor

children.title: The Offer
children.summary: Edric summons Milo again and, without saying it plainly, offers the climb: a clean report, a bigger desk, a path upward like his own. Milo hears his own instinct in the Lich's measured voice and sees, in Edric's refusal of the onward, how afraid the Lich is.
children.setting: The corner office

children.title: The Signature Sheet
children.summary: Back at his desk, Milo cannot stand himself and tears up the report. He asks Zara what the alternative is, and she slides a signature sheet across the partition: a union of the dead and a procedurally impeccable work stoppage. Milo picks up the pen and signs, choosing to refuse the climb.
children.setting: Reconciliations, across the partition
children.tone: Quiet, decisive, the first warmth between them

nodes.title: Procedurally Impeccable
nodes.summary: Zara organizes the signatures and Milo works the ledger. Together they reconcile every soul the Pipeline sent under and file the restructuring of Edric Thane's own account through Reconciliations, by the Pipeline's own rules. The all-staff email announcing the work stoppage is drafted and, for once, completely honest.

children.title: Signatures
children.summary: Zara takes Milo through the Marrow District as she collects signatures. Prava signs and adds her forbidden ledger of names to the evidence, and the despairing Retention team signs one by one. Old Fen will not sign, but files the form correctly for them. Milo sees solidarity, the thing the performance curve was built to prevent, take shape on paper.
children.setting: Intake, Retention and Records across the Marrow District

children.title: Restoring Bell
children.summary: Milo works the ledger backwards, reconciling every soul the Pipeline sent under and starting with Halvard Bell, whose tenure he moves back to where it belongs. The same gift for clean numbers that made him good at the harvest now unmakes it.
children.setting: Milo's desk in Reconciliations, late

children.title: Filed Against the Top
children.summary: Milo and Zara file the restructuring of Edric Thane's own account through Reconciliations, by the rules Edric spent six centuries enforcing, so the pooled account is due to be zeroed. Milo writes his own resignation to go with it.
children.setting: Reconciliations

children.title: Completely Honest
children.summary: Zara and Milo draft the all-staff email announcing the work stoppage, and it says, for once, exactly what the Pipeline does. Milo's finger hovers over send, and then the quarterly review is on the calendar.
children.setting: Reconciliations

nodes.title: Quarterly Review
nodes.summary: At the quarterly review, Milo stands in the corner office and hands Edric Thane a single sheet: his own resignation, with the reconciliation of every sent-under soul attached. Edric reads it, understands it completely and files it correctly, and goes onward. Milo has his boredom back and Zara has company, and the Pipeline must explain itself in plain language.

children.title: The One Sheet
children.summary: Milo stands in the corner office, refusing the chair again, and hands Edric Thane a single sheet of paper: his resignation, with the procedurally flawless reconciliation of every sent-under soul attached. The ledger on Edric's desk is no longer the only one that counts.
children.setting: The corner office, at the quarterly review

children.title: Filed Correctly
children.summary: Edric reads it and understands completely that a clerk has been undone by a clerk, according to the terms of service. He does not argue. He initials, files it correctly, and the pooled account is zeroed. Milo watches the Lich go onward, to wherever the dead go, no longer bored.
children.setting: The corner office

children.title: Plain Language
children.summary: The honest email goes out to all staff, and the Pipeline has to explain to its customers, in plain language, what it does. Back at the partition Milo finds his boredom again and recognises it as the wound where his questions used to be. Zara, for once, looks up, and has company.
children.setting: Reconciliations

w9_outline.about: run-W9's outline (eval-cel book of polyphony_w9; its outline:beats answers hash to the signed W9.json). Bell is sent under in chapter 2, as the source has him: the W10-1 (R) no-finding row. `characters` are names (portable_outline's shape); node ids dropped.

bell.line: Zeroing Out: Zara walks him through closing a restructured account: review the tenure, zero it, file it under. Milo is fast and clean at it, enjoys the satisfaction of a balanced form, and by the end of his first quarter is the best closer on the floor.

nodes.title: Retained
nodes.summary: Milo Voss dies mid-complaint on a Tuesday and wakes in the intake atrium, where Prava's practiced warmth, a laminated org chart and the word 'culture fit' persuade him to accept a post in Reconciliations before anyone offers him a choice. He learns the vocabulary of tenure, quotas and graduation, and feels, for the first time in decades, useful.

children.title: A Meeting That Could Have Been an Email
children.summary: Milo dies mid-sentence on a Tuesday, still complaining about a meeting, and opens his eyes not in nothing but in a queue; the shock is replaced almost at once by the comfort of being given a ticket number.
children.setting: His old office, then the intake atrium of the Undeath Pipeline

children.title: Culture Fit
children.summary: Prava slides a laminated org chart across a laminate desk, tells Milo he has been retained and that his forty-one years of process optimisation are a strong culture fit, and he says yes to Reconciliations before anyone thinks to offer a choice; for the first time in decades he feels seen.
children.setting: Prava's intake desk in the atrium
children.tone: Warm on the surface, quietly ominous

children.title: Orientation Vocabulary
children.summary: Milo learns the words he will live by: tenure, accrued quarter by quarter and spent on the hope of moving on; quotas; graduation; restructuring, which nobody defines. He collects his lanyard eager to start Monday, mistaking his own boredom for a qualification.
children.setting: An orientation room on the edge of the Marrow District

threads: Milo's boredom mistaken for a personality

nodes.title: Initial Here
nodes.summary: Trained by his flat, unexplaining desk neighbour Zara Okafor, Milo discovers with real pleasure that he is superb at zeroing out restructured accounts, and sits through an all-hands where the quarter's one graduation is celebrated with dissolving confetti. Closing a routine file, he finds the tenure does not reconcile: it is draining upward into a single pooled account at the top of the org chart.

children.title: The Desk Neighbour
children.summary: Milo meets Zara Okafor, his trainer, who answers his eager questions in single flat sentences and never looks up; he mistakes her courtesy for friendship and resolves to win her over by being excellent.
children.setting: Adjacent desks in Reconciliations, Marrow District

children.title: Zeroing Out
children.summary: Zara walks him through closing a restructured account: review the tenure, zero it, file it under. Milo is fast and clean at it, enjoys the satisfaction of a balanced form, and by the end of his first quarter is the best closer on the floor.
children.setting: Reconciliations, under gray fluorescent light

children.title: All-Hands
children.summary: In the bedrock amphitheatre the quarter's single graduation is announced to dissolving confetti and someone mentions that the numbers go up to the CEL; Milo assumes it is a department, and when he says so, Zara does not correct him.
children.setting: The all-hands amphitheatre carved from bedrock

children.title: It Does Not Reconcile
children.summary: Closing a routine restructured account, Milo finds the tenure being zeroed is not disappearing but draining upward, faster than labour can explain, into a single pooled account at the top of the org chart. He looks over the partition; Zara, for once, is watching him.
children.setting: Milo's desk in Reconciliations, late in a quarter with no clocks

threads: the CEL mistaken for a department

nodes.title: Low-Hanging Fruit
nodes.summary: Milo traces the pooled account through Records with the help of Old Fen, whose contentment he envies, and learns that the CEL is not a department but Edric Thane, the Chief Executive Lich, who continues on the harvested hope of every soul sent under. His first instinct is to write it up as a process improvement and be seen for it; Zara says only that he should sit with it.

children.title: The Man Who Files Himself
children.summary: Milo takes the pooled account's routing codes down to Records, where Old Fen, so long at his post that he has begun to file himself, cheerfully retrieves the chain for him; Milo envies the old man's untroubled contentment and, for a moment, wants it more than the answer.
children.setting: The endless stacks of Records

children.title: Three Letters
children.summary: The chain of transfers terminates in the office at the top of the org chart, and the archived charter beneath it spells the abbreviation out: the CEL is not a department but the Chief Executive Lich, Edric Thane, a clerk six hundred years dead who continues on the tenure harvested from every soul sent under. Milo understands that the accounts he closes are meals.
children.setting: A sealed archive drawer in Records

children.title: A Process Improvement
children.summary: Back at his desk Milo, energised, drafts a memo framing the harvest as a reconciliation inefficiency he has identified end-to-end and would love to own; he reads it to Zara expecting approval, and she tells him only to sit with it, which lands harder than any argument.
children.setting: Reconciliations, after the floor has emptied

nodes.title: Retention
nodes.summary: Flagged as wavering, Milo is counselled back onto schedule by Halvard Bell of Retention, whose cheer is plainly despair, and stumbles on Prava's forbidden private ledger of eleven thousand names; he sees in his own draft report the first rung of Edric Thane's climb. Realising the Lich stayed in the Marrow District because he fears the onward, Milo tears up the report and tells Zara he is in.

children.title: Wellness Check
children.summary: His closing rate dips and Milo is flagged as wavering; Halvard Bell of Retention, a former dentist ninety years on the team, counsels him back onto schedule with relentless cheer, and Milo hears plainly the despair under every upbeat phrase and recognises his own voice in it.
children.setting: A Retention consultation booth with a motivational poster

children.title: Eleven Thousand Names
children.summary: Returning a form to Intake, Milo finds Prava's forbidden private ledger listing every one of the eleven thousand souls she has onboarded, his own name among them, with the restructured ones marked in her careful hand; she asks him not to report it, and he realises he is the one who closed many of those lines.
children.setting: Prava's intake desk after hours

children.title: The First Rung
children.summary: Rereading his draft memo, Milo sees it for what it is: the first rung of the climb Edric Thane once made, a clerk turning other souls' hope into his own continuance. And he grasps the crack Zara has been waiting for him to see: if the onward were real reward, the Lich would have taken it centuries ago; he stayed because he is afraid of it.
children.setting: Milo's desk in Reconciliations

children.title: I'm In
children.summary: Milo tears up the memo, walks it to the shredder that nobody ever explained, and tells Zara he wants in on whatever she has been building; she slides him a signature sheet without looking up, and he chooses the union of the dead over the promotion he wanted.
children.setting: Across the partition in Reconciliations

threads: the Lich's fear of the onward

nodes.title: Procedurally Impeccable
nodes.summary: Zara's signature sheets pass desk to desk through Records, Retention and Intake while Milo builds the reconciliation of every soul ever sent under, and together they file the restructuring of Edric Thane's own account through the department built to close accounts. The work stoppage goes out as an all-staff email that is, for once, completely honest, and Milo is summoned to the corner office for his quarterly review.

children.title: Signature Sheets
children.summary: Zara's sheets move desk to desk: Old Fen signs in his perfect filing hand, Halvard Bell signs and for once stops smiling, Prava signs with the name of every soul she remembers beside her own. Milo watches the dead discover they are not alone, and the fear the performance curve was built to scatter begins to pool.
children.setting: Records, Retention and Intake, one desk at a time

children.title: Every Soul Sent Under
children.summary: Working nights that have no clocks, Milo builds the reconciliation line by line, restoring the tenure of every soul ever restructured, and finds the last line he must close is the pooled account itself; he files the restructuring of Edric Thane's account through Reconciliations, by the Lich's own rules, with Zara countersigning.
children.setting: Reconciliations, empty but for two desks

children.title: Reply All
children.summary: The work stoppage goes out as an all-staff email that is, for once, completely honest, and across the Marrow District the dead stop hoping on schedule; within the hour a summons arrives for Mr. Voss's quarterly review in the corner office, and Zara tells him, flatly, to bring the paperwork.
children.setting: The Reconciliations floor as every screen lights up

nodes.title: Onward
nodes.summary: In the office no employee returns from unchanged, Milo hands Edric Thane his resignation with the full reconciliation attached, and the Lich, a clerk undone by a clerk under his own terms of service, reviews it, finds it correct, files it and goes onward. Milo gets his boredom back and understands it was a wound where his questions used to be; Zara gets company; and the Pipeline must at last tell its customers, in plain language, what it does.

children.title: The Office at the Top
children.summary: Milo enters the room no employee returns from unchanged and meets Edric Thane, formal and courteous, who speaks to him in ledger metaphors as one clerk to another and offers him the climb: a pooled account of his own. Milo recognises himself in the offer and, for the first time, declines a promotion.
children.setting: The CEL's corner office at the top of Aeon Holdings

children.title: A Single Sheet
children.summary: Milo hands over his resignation with the full reconciliation attached. Edric reviews it slowly, as a clerk would, finds no error, and admits what he has feared for six centuries; then, because the terms of service require it, he files it correctly, and his pooled account zeroes out.
children.setting: Across the CEL's desk

children.title: Plain Language
children.summary: Edric Thane goes onward and the office is only an office. Milo returns to Zara's desk, where she looks up at him; Prava reads the first plain-language notice the Pipeline has ever sent its customers, and Milo finds his boredom back, understanding at last it was a wound where his questions used to be.
children.setting: Reconciliations and the intake atrium, after the stoppage

Title: eval-prose-cel

<synopsis>
BORED TO UNDEATH — a synopsis

PART ONE: THE FIRM

Death, it turns out, is not an ending but an onboarding.

When the world's largest afterlife-services conglomerate, Aeon Holdings, quietly
won the exclusive concession to process the recently deceased three centuries
ago, no one living noticed, because no one living was the customer. The customers
arrived already dead, disoriented, and — crucially — in no position to read the
terms of service. Aeon's founding insight was elegant and terrible: a soul, freed
from the friction of a body, is the most efficient labor unit ever devised. It
does not sleep. It does not unionize, historically speaking. It does not age out
of usefulness, because it has already aged out of everything. It simply needs to
be told what to do, and given the faint, renewable hope that doing it well might
one day earn a promotion out of the ledger and into whatever lies beyond the
beyond.

That hope is the product. That hope is the whole business.

Aeon calls its core operation the Undeath Pipeline, and in the internal style
guide the term is always capitalized, always singular, and never — under any
circumstances — described in plain language to a new hire. The Pipeline is the
machinery by which raw grief is refined into shareholder value: intake,
orientation, assignment, extraction, and, for the vanishingly few, "graduation."
Most of the dead never learn what the Pipeline actually pipes, or where. They
learn their department. They learn their quota. They learn the difference between
a billable haunting and a non-billable one, and they learn not to ask what
happens to the souls whose contracts are "restructured."

The afterlife economy runs on a single currency, called tenure, which is accrued
by labor and spent on the only thing the dead still want: the possibility of
moving on. You cannot buy tenure. You cannot steal it, though people try. You can
only earn it, quarter by quarter, in the gray fluorescent light of the Marrow
District, the vast subterranean office park where the Pipeline's clerical work is
done. The Marrow District has no windows, because there is nothing outside it to
see, and no clocks, because time is a benefit reserved for management.

There is a culture to the place, and the culture is the cruelest technology Aeon
ever built. New hires are given a lanyard, a desk, and a mentor, and the mentor is
always someone three quarters of the way to burning out, because a soul who still
believes is a poor teacher of resignation. There are all-hands meetings, held in
an amphitheater carved from a single slab of the bedrock beneath the Marrow
District, at which the quarter's graduation — always exactly one, always announced
with confetti that dissolves before it lands — is celebrated as proof that the
system works. There are performance reviews, calibrated on a curve so that
someone must always be failing, so that the fear is evenly distributed and never
pools into anything as dangerous as solidarity. There are team-building
exercises. There is a newsletter. The newsletter is the worst part, and everyone
agrees, quietly, at the coffee station that dispenses a gray liquid the dead drink
out of habit rather than need, that the newsletter is the worst part, and no one
ever says so where it could be documented.

The departments spread out from the Pipeline like rings of a felled tree.
Intake greets the newly dead and sorts them by exploitable virtue. Orientation
teaches them the vocabulary that will keep them from ever describing their
situation accurately. Assignment matches a soul's dearest surviving habit to the
task that will grind it down most efficiently: the meticulous go to Records, the
loyal go to Retention, the curious — the dangerous, curious ones — go to
Reconciliations, where curiosity is spent closing the accounts of the disappeared
until there is none left. Above them all floats Management, a stratum of the dead
so thoroughly graduated-in-spirit that they no longer remember wanting to leave,
and above Management, alone, the office at the top.

At the very top of Aeon Holdings sits an office that no employee has ever
entered and returned from unchanged. The being who occupies it holds a title so
old that it has worn down, through centuries of memos and org charts and
mandatory compliance trainings, into a three-letter abbreviation that new hires
mistake, understandably, for the name of a subsidiary or a line of business. They
hear "the CEL" and they picture a department — Corporate something, Logistics
something — and they are not corrected, because the misunderstanding is useful.
The CEL is not a department. The CEL is a person, or was one, a very long time
ago. The letters stand for Chief Executive Lich, and the Lich is real, and the
Lich is watching the numbers.

This is a story about three of the dead, and about what happens to a machine
built on hope when the people inside it finally, quietly, stop hoping.

PART TWO: THE NEW HIRE

Milo Voss died the way most people do: unremarkably, mid-sentence, on a Tuesday,
while complaining about a meeting that could have been an email. In life he had
been a mid-level operations analyst for a company that made a component that went
into a component that went into something no one could name, and he had been, by
his own cheerful admission, extraordinarily good at a job that did not matter. He
had spent forty-one years optimizing processes whose purpose he never questioned,
and he had been comfortable, and he had been bored, and the boredom had felt, at
the time, like a personality.

So when Milo Voss opened his eyes in the intake atrium of the Undeath Pipeline
and a caseworker slid a laminated org chart across a laminate desk and explained,
in the warm and terrible voice of onboarding everywhere, that he had been
retained, that his skills were a strong culture fit, and that he would be
starting Monday in Reconciliations — Milo felt something he had not felt in
decades. He felt seen. He felt, God help him, useful. The afterlife had looked at
his forty-one years of pointless optimization and decided they were an asset, and
Milo Voss, who had never in his life or death been told that his boredom was
valuable, said yes before anyone thought to offer him a choice.

It takes him the better part of a fiscal year to understand what he has agreed
to. Reconciliations, he learns, is the department that closes the accounts of
souls whose contracts have been restructured — that reviews their remaining
tenure, zeroes it out, and files the paperwork that sends them not onward, but
under, into the part of the Pipeline that the style guide will not name. Milo has
been hired, on the strength of his gift for not asking questions, to be very good
at the one job in the afterlife that ought to require asking every question there
is. And he is good at it. That is the horror of the middle of this book: Milo Voss
is good at it, and he likes being good at it, and the liking lasts almost until
the end.

PART THREE: THE ORGANIZER

Zara Okafor has been dead for two hundred and six years, and she has spent almost
all of them angry.

She died young, in a factory fire that the living world found regrettable and the
Pipeline found routine, and she arrived in the Marrow District with the one trait
Aeon Holdings has never found a way to refine out of a soul: she could not stop
noticing who was getting hurt. Two centuries of noticing have made her the most
dangerous kind of employee — the kind who has read the entire contract, including
the appendices, including the parts printed in the ink that only shows up under
grief. Zara knows what the Pipeline pipes. She has known for a hundred years. What
she has never had is leverage, because a soul alone has none, and the dead, Aeon
has made very sure, are always alone.

Zara Okafor is Milo's desk neighbor. She is assigned to train him, and she does,
flawlessly, with a flat professional courtesy that Milo mistakes for friendship
and then, slowly, comes to understand is something far more patient and far more
frightening: recruitment. Zara has spent decades identifying the one structural
weakness in the Undeath Pipeline, and it is not a vault or a password or a
weapon. It is a job. It is Reconciliations. Whoever controls the department that
closes the accounts controls the one ledger the Lich actually reads. And Zara has
just been handed a brand-new Reconciliations analyst who is lonely, and gifted,
and bored, and who has no idea yet that he is the most important soul in the
building.

PART FOUR: THE LICH IN THE CORNER OFFICE

Edric Thane was the third son of a minor merchant house, and he was, in life, a
clerk. This is the joke the whole novel is built on and the reason it aches: the
most powerful being in the afterlife, the Chief Executive Lich, the CEL whose
initials terrify every new hire, was once exactly what Milo Voss is now. Edric
Thane died six hundred years ago owing a debt he could not pay, and he was
retained, and he was good at it, and he was ambitious in the specific, grinding,
upward way of a man who has decided that the only escape from a machine is to
own it. He climbed. He reconciled. He restructured. He learned that tenure could
be pooled, and that a soul who controlled enough pooled tenure could purchase
something no clerk was ever meant to have: continuance. Edric Thane did not
graduate out of the Pipeline. He devoured it, and wore it, and became the reason
no one else ever would.

Now he sits at the top of Aeon Holdings, neither living nor properly dead, a
clerk's resentment scaled up to the size of an institution, and he is not cruel
so much as he is thorough. Edric Thane believes, with the total conviction of the
converted, that hope is a renewable resource and that spending it is what it is
for. He is the villain of this book, and he is right about almost everything, and
that is what makes him terrible: he was Milo once. He was Zara's colleague once.
He is what the Pipeline is designed to produce, the one graduate it will permit,
and his continued existence is the proof, filed and notarized, that the way out
is real — for exactly one soul, and never again.

PART FIVE: THE RESTRUCTURING

The plot turns on a routine account. Milo Voss, closing the books on a soul whose
contract has been restructured, notices — because Zara Okafor has spent a year
teaching him, gently, to notice — that the numbers do not reconcile. Tenure is
disappearing from the ledger faster than labor can explain, and it is all flowing
to a single pooled account at the top of the org chart. Milo has found, without
looking for it, the mechanism by which the CEL sustains himself: every soul
"sent under" is not destroyed but harvested, their accrued hope funneled upward to
keep one ancient clerk continuing. The Undeath Pipeline is not a business with a
monstrous side effect. The monstrous side effect is the business. Everything else
is overhead.

What Milo does with this knowledge is the spine of the back half of the book. His
first instinct — his forty-one years of instinct, his six-hundred-years-ago
Edric Thane instinct — is to optimize it. To report the discrepancy, to be
useful, to be seen, to climb. Zara lets him sit with that instinct until he
cannot stand himself, and then she offers him the alternative she has spent two
centuries building toward: not a rebellion, not a war, nothing so loud that the
Lich could file it under threat and restructure it away. A work stoppage. A
union of the dead. The one thing a machine that runs on hope cannot survive is
the coordinated, documented, procedurally impeccable refusal of its workforce to
keep hoping on schedule.

They do it the only way that could possibly work: as paperwork. Zara has the
organizing; Milo has the ledger; and between them they turn the CEL's own
bureaucracy into the instrument of his undoing, filing the restructuring of Edric
Thane's account through the very department built to close accounts. The climax is
not a battle. It is a quarterly review. Milo Voss stands in the one office no
employee returns from unchanged and hands the Chief Executive Lich a single sheet
of paper — a resignation, his own, and attached to it, procedurally flawless, the
reconciliation of every soul the Pipeline ever sent under, tenure restored, hope
returned, the pooled account that keeps Edric Thane continuing zeroed out by the
same rules Edric spent six centuries enforcing.

Edric Thane, who was a clerk, is undone by a clerk, according to the terms of
service, and the terrible mercy of the ending is that he understands it
completely, and files it correctly, and goes wherever it is the dead go when they
are finally, at last, allowed to be bored no longer.

The dead do not overthrow Aeon Holdings. That would be a different, easier book.
They do something quieter and harder: they read the contract to the end, together,
and hold the machine to its own word. Milo Voss gets his boredom back, and learns
it was never a personality — it was a wound where his questions used to be. Zara
Okafor gets the one thing two centuries of anger never could: company. And the
Undeath Pipeline, for the first time in three hundred years, has to explain to
its customers, in plain language, exactly what it is that it does.

PART SIX: THE PEOPLE IN THE MARGINS

The book is populated, in its middle chapters, by the small and specific dead who
give the satire its ache. There is Prava, the intake caseworker who onboarded
Milo with such practiced warmth and who, it emerges, has onboarded eleven thousand
souls and remembers the name of every one, and keeps them in a private ledger she
is not permitted to have, and weeps, silently and off the clock, at each
graduation because it is the only proof she has that leaving is possible. There is
Old Fen, who has been in Records so long that he has begun to file himself, whose
tragedy is that he is content, whose contentment is the thing Zara most fears and
Milo most envies. There is the Retention team, cheerful and doomed, whose job is
to talk the wavering out of despair and back onto the schedule, and who are very
good at it, and who are, without exception, the most despairing souls in the
building.

And there is the question the novel keeps in its pocket and never quite lets the
reader forget: what, exactly, is on the other side of graduation? Aeon promises an
"onward." The style guide will not define it. Edric Thane, the one soul to ever
buy his way past the ledger, chose not to take it — chose continuance in the
Marrow District over whatever the onward is — and that choice is the crack in the
Lich the whole plot slides a lever into. Because if graduation were truly the
reward the Pipeline sells, the most powerful being in the afterlife would have
taken it six hundred years ago. Edric Thane stayed. Edric Thane is afraid of the
onward. And a machine whose owner does not believe its own product is a machine
that can be brought down by anyone willing to read that fact out loud.

THEMES AND TEXTURE

At its heart, Bored to Undeath is a workplace comedy that curdles, by degrees,
into a tragedy about complicity — about how the most efficient evil is not the
kind that requires monsters but the kind that requires only competent, tired,
reasonable people who have agreed not to ask the next question. Milo Voss is not a
chosen one; he is a good employee, and the book's argument is that in a system
like the Pipeline those are the same thing until the moment they are not. Zara
Okafor is not a warrior; she is an organizer, and her weapon is not a sword but a
signature sheet, and the book insists, page after page, that this is the more
frightening thing to be, because a sword threatens the Lich and a signature sheet
threatens the terms of service, and the Lich can survive a threat but not a
correctly filed contradiction.

The tone is dry, deadpan, and specific: the horror is administrative, delivered in
the language of quarterly targets and culture fit and "restructuring," and the
comedy comes from the exact, lovingly observed gap between what the Pipeline says
it does and what it does. The undead here do not moan; they attend meetings. The
Lich does not roar; he reviews. The apocalypse, when it comes, comes as paperwork,
and the revolution, when it comes, comes as a work stoppage announced by an
all-staff email that is, for once, completely honest.

The setting — Aeon Holdings, the Undeath Pipeline, the windowless Marrow District,
the currency of tenure, the graduation that may be salvation or may be a nicer
word for the same disappearance — is the novel's central invention and its central
metaphor, and none of it should be flattened into a generic corporate dystopia,
because the specific joke is theological: this is what you get when an institution
designed to shepherd souls decides, quite reasonably, quite gradually, that the
souls are the inventory. The CEL is not a brand. The Pipeline is not a factory.
Milo and Zara and Edric are not archetypes wearing office clothes. They are three
clerks, six centuries apart, discovering the same terrible fork in the same gray
hallway, and choosing, two of them, at last, the harder turn.
</synopsis>

record.answer:
Reconciliations was quieter than Milo had pictured, and he had pictured it quiet. Rows of identical desks ran off under the gray fluorescent light until the light gave up, and every desk had someone at it, and nobody was talking.

His was the fourth desk from the end. Someone had left a fresh pad of forms squared exactly to the corner, and a stapler, and a little card that said WELCOME in a font that had clearly been chosen by committee. Milo set down his coffee, which was gray and steaming and had come out of the machine smelling faintly of nothing, and straightened his lanyard so the photo faced outward. In the photo he was smiling. He tried to match it.

The desk beside his, across a low partition, had a nameplate. ZARA OKAFOR. The woman behind it was typing. She had been typing when he walked up, and she was typing now, and the rhythm did not change by so much as a keystroke.

Milo sat. He adjusted his chair. He adjusted it back. He had rehearsed an opening line on the walk over, something warm but not too warm, collaborative, and now it sat in his mouth like a lozenge he was too polite to swallow.

First impressions, he reminded himself, were a deliverable.
